title: Battle of Chipyong-ni (1951): 5,600 Men in a 360° Perimeter
subtitle: February 13 – 15, 1951

lines: The night of February 13th, 1951. Chipyong-ni, Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province.
Inside a small snow-covered basin, fifty-six hundred American and French soldiers were trapped.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Chinese troops filled every ridge around them, and every road out behind them had been cut.
Chipyong-ni had become a small island in the middle of an enemy sea.
Chinese intelligence reportedly estimated the garrison holding this village at barely a thousand men.
A fight that would be over in a single night. That is what they believed.
But in reality, more than five times that number were dug in inside.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: But inside the ring stood the 23rd Infantry Regiment of the U.S. 2nd Division, and the French Battalion.
And surrounding that ring, according to American records, were elements of five Chinese divisions.
Three days and three nights of savage close combat, with bayonets and grenades.
Yet three days later, it was the Chinese who pulled back first.
The human-wave tactic had not once been stopped head-on in the three months since China entered the war.
So why did it grind to a halt, for the first time, in front of this one small ring?

visual.sub: Three months after China entered the war

lines: The Battle of Chipyong-ni.
This is the story of the men who, instead of breaking out and running, dug in where they stood and held.
In October 1950, Chinese forces crossed the Yalu River and entered the war.
Badly battered at the Chongchon River and the Chosin Reservoir, UN forces began to be driven south.
On January 4th, 1951, Seoul fell into enemy hands once again.
The January Fourth Retreat. Columns of refugees crossed the frozen Han River and stretched endlessly south.
scenes.label: U.S. Marines resting by a snowy road (1951)

lines: The Chinese moved only at night, slipping around through the mountains to cut off the roads behind.
Among the soldiers spread a dread that the Chinese simply could not be beaten.
It was at this moment that Lieutenant General Matthew Ridgway took over the U.S. Eighth Army.
He arrived at the end of December 1950, after his predecessor, General Walker, was killed in a jeep accident.
Ridgway believed that destroying enemy strength mattered more than holding ground.
From an army that had only known retreat, he demanded that it learn to fight again.

visual.text: KILL THE ENEMY, NOT HOLD GROUND

lines: On January 25th, 1951, Ridgway ordered his first counterattack, under the name Operation Thunderbolt.
UN forces cautiously began probing and pushing north again.
One of the spearheads was the 23rd Infantry Regiment of the U.S. 2nd Division, on the central front.
Its commander was Colonel Paul Freeman.
A calm, seasoned officer who had led this regiment since the Naktong River line.
And attached to this regiment was one very special unit.
The French Battalion of the United Nations, led by Lieutenant Colonel Ralph Monclar.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Monclar had in fact been a three-star lieutenant general in the French Army.
A fifty-nine-year-old veteran, he had voluntarily stepped down to lieutenant colonel so he could lead the battalion bound for Korea himself.

visual.name: Ralph Monclar
visual.role: Commander, French Bn (Lt. Col. · former Lt. Gen.)

lines: In 1940, at Narvik in Norway, he had led a Foreign Legion half-brigade into battle, a legendary soldier.
Wounded again and again in two world wars, he had returned to the battlefield every time.
Many of the men who followed him were Second World War veterans and volunteers.
Tough men, unafraid of mountain fighting or night combat.
scenes.label: The French Battalion in Korea

lines: At first, the Americans were reportedly unsure what to make of this unfamiliar French unit.
But that doubt would soon turn into deep respect.
The story you are watching is the record of men who held out to the end inside an encircled ring.
So that this record is never forgotten, please join us with a subscribe and a like.
Then on January 29th, a patrol heading for the Twin Tunnels ran into an ambush.
About five kilometers southeast of Chipyong-ni, there was a valley where the Central Line railway ran through two tunnels.
The Americans called this place the Twin Tunnels.
It overlooked the railway and the road to Wonju, a chokepoint among chokepoints.
The patrol drove its trucks up near the tunnels and was pinned down by fire pouring in from the surrounding hills.
After holding on for hours, clinging to the radio, only some of them were rescued.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Chinese had been hiding a large force in this area.
It was the 125th Division of the Chinese 42nd Army.
On January 31st, Freeman led the 3rd Battalion and the French Battalion in and seized the hills around the tunnels.
That night, the men dug into the frozen ground and built positions facing every direction.
Before dawn on February 1st, the Chinese surged forward to the sound of bugles and whistles.
Several regiments of the 125th Division fell on the hills one after another.
They meant to surround the Americans and French around the tunnels completely, front and rear.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: One French company position collapsed, and the enemy came right up to the battalion command post.
As ammunition ran low, the French reportedly fixed bayonets and leapt out of their trenches.
On the snowy slopes, men fought hand to hand, close enough to see each other's faces.
The French Battalion retook its lost position and never gave up the hill.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: In the afternoon the clouds lifted, and fighter-bombers began pounding the Chinese on the hills.
And by dusk, the Chinese withdrew, leaving countless bodies behind.
scenes.label: F-51 Mustang fighter-bomber (Korean War)

lines: The Americans recorded counting more than thirteen hundred Chinese bodies in front of their positions alone.
They estimated total Chinese casualties at around thirty-six hundred.
Their own losses came to about two hundred and fifty, including forty-five killed.

visual.note: Twin Tunnels · U.S. records and estimates (Feb. 1, 1951)

lines: It was the first time the Americans and French had stopped a major Chinese assault head-on.
With new confidence, the 23rd Regiment headed for a small crossroads village to the northwest.
On February 3rd, the regiment moved into Chipyong-ni.
Roads to Yangpyeong, Yeoju and Wonju met here, and the Central Line railway had its Chipyong station.
The regiment immediately began surveying the hills around the village and choosing its positions.

callouts.text: ROADS + CENTRAL LINE RAILWAY = THE GATEWAY

lines: Losing it would open the gateway to the entire central front to the enemy.
For Ridgway, Chipyong-ni was a wedge he simply had to hold.

callouts.text: THE WEDGE OF THE CENTRAL FRONT

lines: But the terrain was the worst possible.
The village sat in a basin barely a hundred meters above sea level, ringed by mountains three to four hundred meters high.
Eight high hills looked down on Chipyong-ni.
To hold every one of those ridgelines would have taken a defensive line some nineteen kilometers around.
It was far too long for the troops Freeman had.
So he gave up the high ground, and drew a small circle linking the low hills around the village.
A circular perimeter roughly one and a half kilometers across.
The 1st Battalion held the north, the 3rd the east, the 2nd the south, and the French Battalion the west.
At the center of the circle sat the artillery and the reserve.
105 and 155 millimeter howitzers, and even anti-aircraft guns, could swing their barrels in any direction.

callouts.text: GUNS AT THE CENTER · FIRE IN ALL DIRECTIONS

lines: Above all, the anti-aircraft unit's quad machine-gun half-tracks could pour a staggering curtain of fire onto troops on the ground.
The soldiers reportedly called that terrifying firepower the meat chopper.
scenes.label: M16 quad .50 anti-aircraft half-track (Korean War)

lines: Wherever the line was breached, the reserve inside could reach it within minutes.
The small, tight circle was, in itself, one great fortress.
scenes.label: 155 mm howitzer firing (Korean War)

lines: The men broke the frozen earth with pickaxes, digging foxholes and connecting trenches.
They strung barbed wire, and laid trip flares in front of their positions that would light up at a touch.
Trenches linked the positions, so ammunition and wounded could move between them out of the enemy's line of fire.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Meanwhile, the situation outside was deteriorating fast.
On the night of February 11th, the Chinese launched what became known as their Fourth Phase Offensive.
North of Hoengseong, the ROK 8th Division was badly mauled and collapsed, and UN forces were pushed back toward Wonju.
The 23rd Regiment at Chipyong-ni was left jutting out ahead, all on its own.
At Hoengseong alone, it was a disastrous defeat in which thousands of South Korean and American troops were killed or captured.
On February 13th, patrols and aerial observers reported Chinese troops converging from every direction.
One by one, the roads into the village began to be cut.

callouts.text: FEB. 13 · ROADS CUT ONE BY ONE

lines: Freeman proposed pulling back south toward Yeoju.
But Ridgway was adamant. Hold Chipyong-ni.
Ridgway promised that even if the regiment was surrounded, he would send a relief force.
Freeman told his men: we will stay here, and fight it out.

visual.text: “WE'LL STAY HERE AND FIGHT IT OUT”

lines: When the sun went down, a strange silence settled over the mountains around the basin.
Fifty-six hundred men held their breath in frozen foxholes, staring into the dark.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: And at ten o'clock on the night of February 13th, the first bugle sounded.
The Chinese surged in from the north, the northwest and the southeast all at once.
Soon the perimeter was under attack from every direction, a full three hundred and sixty degrees.

chapter.title: THE NIGHT OF SIRENS AND BAYONETS

lines: Bugles, whistles and gongs tore through the darkness.
When one line fell, another came on behind it, climbing over its fallen comrades.
All night long, the Chinese probed here and there, searching for a weak spot in the line.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Each time a flare burst, Chinese soldiers in quilted cotton uniforms were exposed on the snow.
Machine guns and mortars fired without pause into that white light.
scenes.label: Trip flare over the front (1951 · reference photo)

lines: The guns at the center of the circle kept turning in every direction, firing round after round.
Inside an encircled ring, whichever way you faced, the front line was right in front of you.
scenes.label: 155 mm howitzer in action (Korean War)

lines: The most famous scene played out on the west side, in the French Battalion's sector.
A mass of Chinese troops had pushed right up to the edge of the French trenches.
At that moment, a piercing mechanical wail rose from the French lines.
It was a hand-cranked siren.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: As the siren drowned out the bugles, the French fixed bayonets and charged out of their trenches.
Hurling grenades and shouting, they plunged straight into the middle of the enemy.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: A sound no one expected, and bayonets coming straight at them.
The Chinese ranks scattered, and the western sector held to the end.
Bugles and gongs had been the enemy's weapons of terror.
Monclar's men had, in effect, answered them with a siren.
At dawn on February 14th, the Chinese fell back into the hills, leaving their dead behind.
The first night had been survived. But it was only the beginning.
That day, Colonel Freeman himself was wounded in the leg by mortar fragments.
Even so, he limped around the perimeter and never stopped commanding.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Ammunition and food were running out fast.
When daylight came, transport planes flew over and dropped supplies by parachute into the circle.
scenes.label: Troops receiving air-dropped supplies (1951)

lines: Some of the bundles landed outside the perimeter, inside the enemy's field of fire.
Men who climbed out of their foxholes to retrieve them were sometimes cut down by snipers.

visual.accent: RETRIEVED AT THE RISK OF LIFE

lines: Helicopters brought in ammunition and medical supplies, and flew the badly wounded out on the way back.
They were the only thread linking the encircled ring to the outside world.
scenes.label: H-5 helicopter evacuating wounded (1951)

lines: The same day, to the southeast at Wonju, Chinese columns moving down along the Som River were caught in massed UN artillery fire.
With this barrage, which the Americans called the Wonju Shoot, the Chinese were stopped on the Wonju front as well.
On the night of February 14th, the Chinese came again in even greater numbers.
Attacks that began around midnight hammered the north, the east and the west in turn.
This time the attacks were bigger and more relentless, covered by mortars and machine guns.

callouts.text: NIGHT OF FEB. 14 · SECOND GENERAL ASSAULT

lines: In the east, Company I of the 3rd Battalion was overrun for a time,
but its men counterattacked and quickly took the position back.
Sergeant First Class William Sitman of Company M threw himself on a grenade that landed in his machine-gun position.
His sacrifice saved five of his comrades, and he was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.

visual.accent: SFC WILLIAM S. SITMAN · CO. M

lines: Then the assaults began to concentrate on the south, the sector held by the 2nd Battalion.
Wave after wave of the enemy pressed against the foxholes of Company G on the southern hill.
Private First Class Bruno Orig of Company G stayed alone on his machine gun to buy time for his comrades to pull back.
He was killed where he stood, and he too would receive the Medal of Honor.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Before dawn on February 15th, the Company G position finally fell.
The Chinese poured down from the direction of Hill 397 and drove into the southern side of the ring.
If the gap could not be sealed, the whole perimeter might collapse from the inside.
Freeman scraped together his last reserve, the Ranger company, along with men from other companies, and sent them to counterattack.
But after hand-to-hand fighting on the snowy slope, the counterattack failed.
Even after daybreak, the Chinese who had taken the southern hill would not budge.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Ammunition was nearly gone, and the hole in the south could not be closed.
The only hope left was a relief force coming up from the south.

visual.accent: A RELIEF FORCE FROM THE SOUTH

lines: At that very hour, to the south, near Yeoju,
the 5th Cavalry Regiment of the U.S. 1st Cavalry Division was fighting its way north toward Chipyong-ni.
It was the very relief force Ridgway had promised.
But on foot, they could never reach Chipyong-ni before nightfall.
The regimental commander, Colonel Marcel Crombez, decided to punch through the enemy with tanks alone.
Thirteen M46 Patton tanks and ten M4 Shermans, twenty-three in all.
And clinging to the tanks were a hundred and sixty infantrymen of Company L.
The battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Treacy, objected to putting infantry on top of the tanks, but Crombez did not change his decision.
scenes.label: Tanks supporting infantry (Korean War)

lines: At three forty-five in the afternoon of February 15th, the column entered the narrow valley road leading through Koksu-ri.
About ten kilometers remained to Chipyong-ni.
Machine guns, mortars and rockets rained down from the hills on both sides.
The tanks kept racing on without stopping, and each time, infantrymen clinging to them were thrown off onto the road.
Passing through Koksu-ri, Crombez's column was forced to halt twice.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: When the lead tank was hit and stopped, Crombez drove his own tank forward to lead the column.
Stop, and everyone dies. That was his calculation.
About a mile south of Chipyong-ni, in front of a small village called Masan,
the tanks slammed head-on into the Chinese dug in on the hills along both sides of the road.
Tank guns and machine guns swept the trenches on the hills one by one.
Inside the perimeter, the 23rd Regiment attacked the southern hill again, and the Chinese were caught between front and rear.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Around five in the afternoon, Crombez's tanks finally rolled into the Chipyong-ni perimeter.
Inside the encircled ring, the men erupted in cheers.
The relief tanks had struck the Chinese holding the south side of the perimeter squarely from behind.
But the price was high.
Of the hundred and sixty infantrymen who had set out on the tanks, only about twenty-three reached Chipyong-ni.

visual.note: TF Crombez infantry · U.S. records (Feb. 15, 1951 · arrival figures vary)

lines: Many of the men left behind on the road were killed or captured.
To this day, Crombez's decision is debated, somewhere between a brave breakthrough and a reckless sacrifice.
That night, the Chinese lifted the encirclement and began withdrawing north.
And so the three-day siege came to an end.
Blocked at both Wonju and Chipyong-ni at once, the Chinese Fourth Phase Offensive lost its momentum.
On the morning of February 16th, when the soldiers stepped out of their perimeter into the falling snow,
abandoned weapons and equipment lay scattered endlessly across every slope.
And among them, covered by snow, lay countless Chinese soldiers who would never return home.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: How did fifty-six hundred surrounded men hold off an enemy several times their size?
Why the encircled ring survived.
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, the three-hundred-sixty-degree perimeter.
Because the circle was small and tight, wherever it was breached, the reserve inside could rush there at once.
Freeman's choice to give up the high ground was exactly what made the position so strong.
Second, firepower and the sky.
The artillery at the center of the ring poured out shells for three days straight,
and whenever the weather cleared, fighter-bombers pounded the encirclement while transports and helicopters kept the ring alive.
scenes.label: U.S. air attack on a ground target (Korean War)

lines: Third, the decision to hold.
Ridgway chose to hold rather than retreat.
And Freeman, with his wounded leg, and Monclar, at fifty-nine, fought beside their men to the very end.
Fourth, the armored relief.
Crombez's tanks tore through the encirclement without stopping.
It came at a heavy cost, but that breakthrough saved the southern side just as it was about to collapse.
According to U.S. records, UN forces at Chipyong-ni lost fifty-one killed, two hundred fifty wounded and forty-two missing.
Chinese losses are estimated at around two thousand killed and three thousand wounded, though Chinese records give far lower figures.

visual.note: Casualties · U.S. records and estimates (Feb. 13–15, 1951) · Chinese records lower

lines: For this battle, the 23rd Regiment and the French Battalion received the U.S. Presidential Unit Citation.
It was the moment the Americans' doubt about those unfamiliar French soldiers turned into deep respect.
For the first time since entering the war, the Chinese had clearly backed down in a head-on fight.
From this day on, the fear that had spread among UN troops began to turn into confidence.
A week later, on February 21st, Ridgway went on the offensive with Operation Killer.
And in mid-March, UN forces finally retook Seoul.
That is why Chipyong-ni is called the Gettysburg of the Korean War.
It was the turning point, where the tide of the war reversed.
After Chipyong-ni, the Chinese never again pushed deep south of Seoul.

visual.big: THE GETTYSBURG OF THE KOREAN WAR
visual.sub: Where the tide of war turned

lines: Today, Chipyong-ni has a battle memorial hall and a monument to the French troops.
Every year, ceremonies are held here to honor that victory and that sacrifice.
scenes.label: French memorial, Battle of Chipyong-ni

lines: Freeman later rose to the rank of four-star general in the U.S. Army.
And Monclar passed away in 1964, at the age of seventy-two.
One small circle, once drawn across a snow-covered basin.
Today it lies quietly asleep among the rice paddies and fields of an ordinary village.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Men who could have broken out and run.
Instead they stayed where they were, and even with nothing at their backs, they did not retreat.

items.text: They dug in instead of running
With nothing at their backs, they did not retreat

lines: If this story meant something to you, please subscribe and like.
We will continue these fading records of war in the next story.

visual.title:
February 1951, Chipyong-ni.
Where the human wave was first broken.
